newsitem.title: ITALY: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON ENDS SEASON ON WINNING NOTE.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON ENDS SEASON ON WINNING NOTE.

text.p: Michael Johnson ended his record breaking season on a winning note at the grand prix final on Saturday with his 57th successive victory over 400 metres.

Johnson, who became the first man to win a 200-400 Olympic double in Atlanta and who also set two world 200 metres records during the summer, picked up a $50,000 cheque for his effortless victory in 44.53 seconds in Milan's historic and newly refurbished Arena stadium.
The American, running in shiny purple shoes, cruised through the opening half of the race before stepping up a gear and leading home an American sweep of the first four places.
Anthuan Maybank was second in 45.19, Derek Mills third in 45.24 and Darnell Hall fourth in 45.34.
Britain's Roger Black who took the silver medal behind Johnson in Atlanta was fifth in 45.42 seconds.
Another American Olympic champion to cash in on a great season was 400 hurdles champion Derrick Adkins who won his race in a modest 48.63 seconds to pick up his $50,000 cheque for first place.
That victory also kept him in contention for another possible big cheque at the end of the night.
Adkins finished well clear of compatriot Torrence Zellner and his perennial rival, the Olympic silver medallist Samuel Matete of Zambia who was third in 49.36.

Australian Cathy Freeman, who won the silver medal in Atlanta, took advantage of Olympic champion Marie-Jo Perec's absence to win the women's 400 in 49.60 seconds, holding off a determined finish from Nigerian Falilat Ogunkoya, the Olympic bronze medallist, who was second in 49.73.
Jamaican Merlene Ottey, deprived of the Olympic 100 metres title when she lost on a photo-finish to American Gail Devers made up for that disappointment with a spectacular 100 victory over Devers.
Ottey won in 10.74 seconds the fastest time run by a woman since Florence Griffith Joyner ran 10.62 seconds in a qualifying round on the way to winning the Olympic title in Seoul eight years ago.

Not only was it Ottey's fastest-ever time, four hundredths of a second quicker than her previous best of 10.78 six years go, it lifted her to second in the all-time list of women sprinters as only Griffith-Joyner, with four superior times during 1988, has ever run faster.
Ottey, 35, who has been talking of retiring at the end of this season, brought the capacity 11,000 crowd to its feet as she scorched past Devers in the last 20 metres.
Devers seemed to be heading for victory but Ottey caught and overtook her with a blistering finish to leave Devers second in 10.83 with Nigerian Mary Onyali third in 11.00.

Ottey, beaten by Devers in both the 1993 world championships and the Atlanta Olympics although clocking the same time as the American in both races, could hardly conceal her delight after winning the race and the $50,000 prize money and was eager to pose for photographers next to the scoreboard showing her time.

Canadian Donovan Bailey, the men's Olympic 100 metres champion also had to be content with second place, losing out to American champion Dennis Mitchell who was never headed after blasting out of the blocks, coming home in 9.91 seconds to equal his personal best. Bailey clocked 9.95 with Nigerian Osmond Ezinwa third in 10.05.
Noureddine Morceli was another Atlanta champion forced to concede victory when he was beaten for the second time in his last four races.
It was his first defeat over 1,500 metres or a mile in 56 races since 1992, a signal that his position as the best middle- distance runner in the world is now under serious threat.

Morceli was outpaced in the home straight by Hicham El Guerroudj in the 1,500 metres, the Moroccan gaining some consolation for his fall in the Olympic final which cost him the chance of a medal. His victory deprived Morceli a chance of winning the overall Grand Prix title and earned El Guerroudj $50,000.
El Guerroudj won in three minutes 38.80 seconds to Morceli's 3:39.69 after the Algerian led at the bell.

Svetlana Masterkova of the Soviet Union, who has set world records at 1,000 metres and the mile since winning the 800-1500 double in Atlanta, also ended her season on a high by winning the 1,500 metres in 4:11.42 -- almost 11 seconds slower than her gold-medal time in Atlanta.

Daniel Komen of Kenya, who smashed Morceli's 3,000 metres world record in Rieti last Sunday, ran a tactically excellent 5,000 in 12:52.38 ahead of Salah Hissou of Morocco to not only win that event and $50,000 but also the overall grand prix title worth $200,000.
Ludmilla Engquist of Sweden crowned her golden Olympic year with victory in the 100 metres hurdles in 12.61 seconds and the overall women's title, also pocketing $250,000 in prize money.

While this meet marked the end of the competitive season, around 50 athletes including Morceli, Komen and American Olympic high jump champion Charles Austin are expected to take part in the IAAF Solidarity Meeting in Sarajevo on Monday.
IAAF spokesman Giorgio Reineri said on Saturday: "We do not yet know exactly what athletes will be in Sarajevo, we will wait and see who turns up on the charter flight on Sunday morning."
